final_proof:
The assertion as written depends on the convention for \(\mathbb N\). Under the convention \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), it is false, because the generalized sum in (1) contains the term with index \(0\), whereas the series in (2) does not.

Indeed, let \(V=\mathbb R\), which is a Banach space, and define
\[
v_0=1,\qquad v_n=0\quad(n\ge 1),
\]
and let \(r=1\). For the indexed-family interpretation of the generalized sum, its absolute finite-sum net is
\[
A_F=\sum_{n\in F}\lVert v_n\rVert
\qquad(F\subseteq\mathbb N\text{ finite}),
\]
where the finite subsets are directed by inclusion. If \(F\supseteq\{0\}\), then \(A_F=1\). Thus this net is eventually equal to \(1\), and so the generalized sum is absolutely net convergent to \(r=1\). If the braces in (1) are instead read literally as the range set, that range is \(\{0,1\}\), and the corresponding finite-subset net is likewise eventually equal to \(|0|+|1|=1\). Thus (1) holds under either reading.

On the other hand,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lVert v_n\rVert
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}0=0.
\]
Consequently \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}v_n\) is not absolutely convergent to \(r=1\). Hence (1) does not imply (2), and the stated equivalence is false when \(0\in\mathbb N\).

A corrected statement is obtained by making the index sets agree: either replace the series in (2) by \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}v_n\), or restrict the generalized sum in (1) to the indices \(n\ge1\). More generally, let
\[
J=\{m,m+1,m+2,\ldots\},
\]
where \(m\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), and interpret the generalized sum as the sum of the indexed family \((v_n)_{n\in J}\), so that equal values at different indices are counted with their multiplicities. Then the generalized sum is absolutely net convergent to \(r\) if and only if the corresponding series \(\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}v_n\) is absolutely convergent to \(r\).

To prove this corrected statement, put \(a_n=\lVert v_n\rVert\ge0\). For each finite \(F\subseteq J\), set
\[
A_F=\sum_{n\in F}a_n,
\]
and for \(N\in J\), set
\[
s_N=\sum_{n=m}^{N}a_n.
\]
Absolute net convergence to \(r\) says that \(A_F\to r\) as the finite subsets \(F\) increase by inclusion, while absolute convergence of the series to \(r\) says that \(s_N\to r\).

Suppose first that \(A_F\to r\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite set \(F_0\subseteq J\) such that
\[
F\supseteq F_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |A_F-r|<\varepsilon.
\]
Choose \(N_0\in J\) such that \(F_0\subseteq\{m,m+1,\ldots,N_0\}\). For every \(N\ge N_0\), the initial segment \(\{m,m+1,\ldots,N\}\) contains \(F_0\), and therefore
\[
|s_N-r|=
\left|A_{\{m,m+1,\ldots,N\}}-r\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
Thus \(s_N\to r\).

Conversely, suppose that \(s_N\to r\). Since all \(a_n\) are nonnegative, \((s_N)\) is increasing. It follows that \(s_N\le r\) for every \(N\): otherwise, if \(s_N>r\) for some \(N\), then \(s_M\ge s_N>r\) for every \(M\ge N\), contradicting \(s_M\to r\).

Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N_0\) such that
\[
0\le r-s_{N_0}<\varepsilon,
\]
and put \(F_0=\{m,m+1,\ldots,N_0\}\). If \(F\subseteq J\) is finite and \(F\supseteq F_0\), choose \(M\) sufficiently large that \(F\subseteq\{m,m+1,\ldots,M\}\). Nonnegativity then gives
\[
s_{N_0}=A_{F_0}\le A_F\le s_M\le r.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|A_F-r|=r-A_F\le r-s_{N_0}<\varepsilon.
\]
Hence \(A_F\to r\), proving the corrected equivalence.

In particular, if the author's convention is \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\), the two index sets in the original statement already agree, and the preceding proof with \(m=1\) proves the original claim verbatim.
